extracted.intended_audience: courts, administrative agencies, agency counsel, litigants and practitioners in administrative law (rulemaking and judicial review)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for courts (and stakeholders) on factors to consider when deciding whether to bar new issues raised for the first time in preenforcement judicial review of agency rulemakings. Focuses on a non‑exclusive checklist of contextual factors, policy considerations, and procedural responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Issue raised by another participant
rubrics_metrics.description: The issue was raised by a participant in the rulemaking other than the litigant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If another participant raised the issue during rulemaking, courts generally will be less likely to invoke issue‑exhaustion to bar judicial review; see Portland Gen. Elec. Co. v. Bonneville Power Admin. The Conference invites courts to consider whether someone else put the agency on notice of the issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Issue addressed by the agency sua sponte
rubrics_metrics.description: The issue was addressed by the agency on its own initiative in the rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the agency considered the issue on its own initiative, exclusion of the issue on exhaustion grounds is less appropriate because the agency had an opportunity to address it; courts should consider whether the agency's own attention to the matter obviates exhaustion concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency failed to address an issue so fundamental it had an affirmative responsibility to address
rubrics_metrics.description: The agency failed to address an issue that was so fundamental to the rulemaking proceeding or to the rule's basis and purpose that the agency had an affirmative responsibility to address it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where an issue is central to the rule's basis or purpose, courts should factor whether the agency owed an affirmative duty to examine and explain that issue (e.g., key assumptions, alternatives, statutory/APA issues); failure to do so counsels against foreclosing review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional objections
rubrics_metrics.description: The issue involves an objection that the rule violates the U.S. Constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutional claims are a distinct category—courts should recognize that extraordinary circumstances may justify permitting a constitutional challenge even if not raised during rulemaking; nevertheless participants should raise constitutional objections during rulemaking when possible so the agency can address or explain the issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Futility of raising the issue during rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: It would have been futile to raise the issue during the rulemaking proceeding because the agency clearly indicated that it would not entertain comments on or objections regarding that issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may excuse exhaustion where it would have been futile to raise the issue, but futility should not lightly be presumed; factual showing of the agency's refusal to consider the topic is required (see WATCH v. FCC and Comite De Apoyo A Los Trabajadores Agricolas v. Solis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural impediments to raising the issue
rubrics_metrics.description: The issue could not reasonably be expected to have been raised during the rulemaking proceeding because of the procedures used by the agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If agency procedures (e.g., informal processes, lack of notice or solicitation of comment on certain matters) prevented reasonable opportunity to raise the issue, courts should consider excusing exhaustion (see Alaska Survival v. Surface Transp. Bd.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing — basis for the objection did not yet exist
rubrics_metrics.description: The basis for the objection did not exist at a time when rulemaking participants could raise it in a timely comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where new facts, law, or circumstances giving rise to an objection postdate the comment period (so participants could not timely have raised it), courts should weigh this timing factor as supporting consideration of the issue despite lack of prior administrative presentation (see CSX Transp. v. STB).

rubrics_metrics.name: Opportunity to show adequate prior presentation or justify non‑exhaustion
rubrics_metrics.description: Litigants should be given an opportunity to demonstrate that some participant adequately raised the issue during the rulemaking or that circumstances exist to justify not requiring issue exhaustion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an exhaustion question arises, courts should permit parties to show (1) adequate prior presentation by another participant or (2) special circumstances justifying waiver; the Conference emphasizes allowing litigants to make this showing before excluding issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency opportunity to respond to newly raised issues
rubrics_metrics.description: If a court declines to apply issue exhaustion and allows new issues, the agency should be given an opportunity to respond to new objections on the merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical remedies include permitting supplemental briefing, allowing the agency to supplement the administrative record, or remanding for limited agency consideration — courts have various options tailored to circumstances (e.g., permit briefing or order remand to solicit agency views).

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy justifications favoring application of issue exhaustion
rubrics_metrics.description: Considerations that support applying the issue exhaustion doctrine to rulemaking: promoting active public participation, orderly resolution of legal and policy issues, fully informed agency decisionmaking, a robust administrative record for judicial review, certainty and finality, and avoidance of post‑hoc rationalizations and disruption of agency work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These benefits may be especially persuasive where the challenged issue concerns factual bases, agency evaluation of alternatives, or the agency's exercise of discretion; courts should weigh these systemic advantages when deciding whether to require exhaustion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy concerns cautioning against overbroad application
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical and doctrinal concerns that counsel limitation of exhaustion: it can create barriers to judicial review for those who did not continuously monitor proceedings, increase burdens on commenters to anticipate all possible future claims, and leave fundamental legal questions unaddressed, producing uncertainty and inefficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should be sensitive to these countervailing harms and avoid an overbroad application of exhaustion developed for adversarial adjudications; balance these concerns against the policy justifications for exhaustion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non‑exclusive checklist / not a fixed doctrinal formula
rubrics_metrics.description: The Conference's list of factors is a checklist of potentially relevant considerations, not a fixed doctrinal formula, and is inapplicable where a statute directs otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should treat the listed factors as flexible guidance—some may be dispositive in particular cases, others irrelevant. Statutory exhaustion requirements override the checklist where Congress has spoken.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural fallback — APA §553(e) petition right
rubrics_metrics.description: Where application of the issue exhaustion doctrine forecloses judicial review, the Administrative Procedure Act, 5 U.S.C. 553(e), provides a procedural mechanism for the public to raise new issues by petitioning agencies for amendment or repeal of rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The right to petition under APA §553(e) is a remedial route the public can use to prompt agency reconsideration when judicial review is barred by exhaustion; courts and parties should be aware of this procedural alternative.
